guide.title: A Red, Red Rose — a guided reading and memorisation plan
guide.description: An unhurried reading of Robert Burns’s poem, with short passages, images, sound and gentle returns to the text.

metadata.chunkingStrategy: Passages within original stanzas; chunks of at most two lines. Read aloud and recall at your own pace, without scored exercises.

poem.title: A Red, Red Rose
poem.author: Robert Burns
poem.text:
O my Luve’s like a red, red rose,
That’s newly sprung in June;
O my Luve’s like the melodie
That’s sweetly play’d in tune.

As fair are thou, my bonie lass,
So deep in luve am I;
And I will luve thee still, my Dear,
Till a’ the seas gang dry.

Till a’ the seas gang dry, my Dear,
And the rocks melt wi’ the sun:
I will luve thee still, my dear,
While the sands o’ life shall run.

And fare thee weel, my only Luve!
And fare thee weel, a while!
And I will come again, my Luve,
Tho’ it were ten thousand mile!

metadata.edition: Scottish Poetry Library text, also printed in University of Glasgow Scottish Literature in the Classroom, p. 7. Four four-line stanzas. Preserve are, bonie, Luve’s and all Scots spellings.

coverImage.alt: Oil painting of a woman beside a stone wall and red rose hedge, looking towards a country path across green fields.

pages.title: An invitation to read
pages.bodyMarkdown: Burns brings a declaration of love into the rhythms of a song. This text keeps its Scots words and spellings. Read luve as love, bonie as lovely, and weel as well. You need not put on an accent: let the returning phrases and the rise and fall of your own voice bring the lines close.

pages.title: Stay with these lines
pages.bodyMarkdown: Read the passage aloud, following the sentence through the line endings. Pause over an image or sound that draws your attention.

pages.title: Flower and melody
pages.bodyMarkdown: The first pair of lines offers something seen; the second, something heard. Both begin with the same affectionate phrase. June and tune give the stanza its answering sounds. Let the longer first and third lines open out, then hear the shorter lines settle. The spelling melodie belongs to the chosen text; say it as melody. Picture freshness in the rose and movement in the music.

pages.title: A returning address
pages.bodyMarkdown: The first and third lines begin alike, and June answers tune. Those returns make the verse easy to carry in the voice. Hear the words as an affectionate address rather than an announcement to a crowd.

pages.title: The scale of a promise
pages.bodyMarkdown: Bonie means lovely; lass means a young woman. The speaker turns from describing the beloved to measuring the depth and duration of his love. The last line imagines all the seas going dry: a’ means all and gang means go. Let the impossible scale emerge naturally from the intimate address. The rhyme of I and dry keeps the personal voice beside that vast image.

pages.title: Sea, rock and sand
pages.bodyMarkdown: The closing image of the previous stanza becomes the opening of this one, with an added address to the beloved. That return is a useful bridge for memory. Wi’ means with; o’ means of. Sea and rock seem immense, but the final line brings us to running sand and the measure of a life. Listen to sun and run, and allow the images to change scale without rushing them.

pages.title: Farewell for a while
pages.bodyMarkdown: The repeated farewell asks for a little space in the voice. Weel means well, and Tho’ means though. The distance in the final line is enormous, but the speaker insists on returning. Keep the source’s singular mile: it answers while in the rhyme. Now read the four stanzas together, following flower and melody, promise, great stretches of time, and the parting itself.
